title: Reading paper: The Palace That Moved (15 questions)
subject: English
source: Written for english/y6 lesson 79 (Teacher's reading paper: The Palace That Moved (an original passage about the Crystal Palace's move to Sydenham and the 1936 fire, with 15 questions; written for this assessment; in the portal and printable))
intro: Lesson 79. Summer 1 reading assessment. Read the passage carefully, then answer every question. Check the marks to see how much to write.

passage.title: The Palace That Moved
paras: In 1851, a building made almost entirely of glass rose in Hyde Park, London. It was designed by Joseph Paxton, a gardener who had built glasshouses for plants, and it was so bright and sparkling that people called it the Crystal Palace. Inside was the Great Exhibition, where over six million visitors came to marvel at machines, inventions and treasures from around the world.

When the exhibition closed, the building was not thrown away. Instead, it was taken apart piece by piece, carried across London and rebuilt, even larger, on a hill at Sydenham in the south of the city. It reopened in 1854, surrounded by gardens, fountains and life-sized models of dinosaurs, which can still be seen in the park today.

For more than eighty years, the Crystal Palace was a place of wonder. There were concerts, shows and exhibitions, and on a clear day its glass could be seen shining from miles away. The crowds fell silent as the doors swung open on special days, gazing up at the great curved roof.

Then, on the night of 30 November 1936, a small fire started inside. Within hours, the whole palace was ablaze. The glow lit up the sky so brightly that it could be seen across London, and thousands of people came to watch. By morning, only twisted iron and melted glass remained.

The palace was never rebuilt, but its name lives on. The area of London where it stood is still called Crystal Palace, and visitors can walk in the park, see the stone dinosaurs and imagine the glittering building that once stood on the hill.

questions.q: In which year was it built in Hyde Park?
Why was it called the Crystal Palace?
questions.a: It was made almost entirely of glass and was bright and sparkling.

questions.q: How many visitors came to the Great Exhibition?

questions.a: On a hill at Sydenham in south London

questions.q: Find and copy a word in paragraph 2 that shows it was taken apart carefully.
What could visitors see in the gardens at Sydenham? Give two things.
questions.a: Any two: gardens, fountains, life-sized models of dinosaurs.

questions.q: 'The crowds fell silent as the doors swung open.' How did the crowds feel? Give evidence.
questions.a: Awed or amazed: they 'fell silent', which suggests they were overwhelmed.

questions.q: How do we know the fire was very big? Give two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: It could be seen across London; thousands came to watch; only twisted iron and melted glass remained.

questions.q: Why do you think the writer describes the 'twisted iron and melted glass'?
questions.a: To show how completely the fire destroyed the palace, contrasting with its earlier sparkle.

questions.q: Explain how the writer shows the palace was special for many years. Use a point, evidence and explanation.
questions.a: Point: it was a place of wonder; evidence: 'concerts, shows and exhibitions' and its glass 'could be seen shining from miles away'; explanation: people visited for many kinds of events and it was a famous landmark.

questions.q: How does the last paragraph end the passage?
questions.a: It shows the palace's name and park live on, ending on a hopeful note after the fire.

questions.q: Summarise the passage in one sentence.
questions.a: The glass Crystal Palace was built for the Great Exhibition, moved to Sydenham and destroyed by fire in 1936, but its name lives on.
